The upcoming MacBook Ultra has never been expected to come cheap, featuring a brand-new, thinner design with an OLED and touchscreen display—even before factoring in price hikes driven by rising memory costs, the price tag is already steep. And according to the latest report, manufacturing costs may be pushed even higher.

Apple has always preferred to source components from multiple suppliers to maximise display reliability and give itself greater leverage to negotiate the best prices. It had originally hoped to continue this approach with the MacBook Ultra. However, according to supply chain sources, Apple has decided to use only one display supplier……

Apple has three display partners across its product line: Samsung, LG, and BOE (京東方). Of these, BOE has so far only supplied screens for the company's lower-end products, while higher-end display orders are shared between Samsung and LG.

The MacBook Ultra will feature the most sophisticated display ever fitted to an Apple product. Combining stacked OLED with touchscreen technology and applying it to the larger sizes required by a laptop is no easy feat. According to the latest supply chain report, Apple has decided that these screens will be supplied exclusively by Samsung.

Korean media outlet The Elec reports that LG failed to meet Apple's required production volumes.

Apple demanded the use of larger substrates for mass production. Samsung Display responded with its 8.6th-generation OLED production line, while LG Display was reportedly considering continuing to use its existing 6th-generation production line. Even the 6th-generation line can produce OLED panels for laptops, but it falls short of the 8.6th-generation line in both substrate efficiency and output. Because initial production volumes were too low, Apple ultimately chose Samsung Display as its exclusive supplier.

It seems LG's limited production capacity cannot offset the additional logistical complexity that comes with using two suppliers. It is expected that the company will not be able to supply screens for this flagship MacBook before 2029.

This arrangement clearly gives Samsung a much stronger bargaining position on panel prices, which is expected to drive up Apple's manufacturing costs. Apple is very likely to pass these expenses on to consumers, just as it has done with the more expensive memory costs.

Given how eye-wateringly expensive the MacBook Ultra's price tag could be, how likely are you to consider upgrading? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
